data.title: Prašník – Tlstá hora, a Hallstatt hillfort by the mountain pass
data.excerpt: A lesser-known hillfort on the summit of Tlstá hora, 3.5 km east of Prašník, built in the Early Iron Age by the people of the Kalenderberg culture. From the site comes an exceptional early La Tène iron belt clasp decorated with griffins and the head of a bird of prey, published by K. Pieta in 2019.
data.metaTitle: Prašník – Tlstá hora, a Hallstatt hillfort
data.metaDescription: A lesser-known hillfort on Tlstá hora near Prašník, 3.5 km from Hrádok, close to an old pass across the Lesser Carpathians, with an early La Tène belt clasp.

children.text: The village of Prašník is known to our readers for its interesting, though already partly destroyed, Slavic

The village lies close to an old pass across the Lesser Carpathians leading from the Trnava Hills to the opposite side of the range. The Hrádok just mentioned lies in the immediate vicinity of this pass. In the village, however, there rises another, less well-known hillfort, 3.5 km to the east, on the summit of a massive rise called Tlstá hora, at spot height 426 m. We date the hillfort to the mystical period of the Early Iron Age (the Hallstatt period) and its builders were evidently the people of the Kalenderberg culture, which in the territory of present-day Slovakia became famous above all through the hillfort of Molpír with its exceptional bronze and pottery finds, as well as through the magnificent painted pottery from the princely Hallstatt barrows at Nové Košariská. Occupation of the hillfort ends at the turn of the Early and the Late (La Tène) Iron Age. Some also call it Babylon.

children.text: The hillfort was excavated in the early 1980s by Petr Novák, a member of staff of the Trnava Museum, who opened 10 trenches here. As regards the appearance and position of the hillfort, Novák writes that part of the eastern slope, with artificially modified terraces, is joined by the defences to the oval upland plateau, which rises 226 m above the Holeška brook flowing through the valley. No defences were identified on the northern and western edges of the hillfort, but the steep hillsides with outcropping rocks of the limestone bedrock, together with a possible timber palisade, provided sufficient protection against any attack by an enemy. The defences on the south-eastern side of the hillfort are unfinished and some 40 metres separate them from the steep northern slope. Originally there was evidently only a palisade there, and it was assumed that the rampart would be completed. The front wall of the rampart was formed of drystone-laid stones; the rampart evidently had a box construction about 170 cm wide. The stone wall of the rampart was approximately 2.30 metres high and it may be assumed (even though the excavation did not succeed in proving it) that a timber palisade was also raised on the crest of the rampart. The excavation confirmed several houses at the hillfort, which evidently had a construction similar to the houses at the above-mentioned hillfort of Molpír at Smolenice: posts with wattle between them daubed with clay.

As for the finds made during the excavation, the largest quantity is pottery, for which we know analogies in the milieu of the Lusatian culture (cups) and also in that of north-eastern Hungary (the Mezocsát culture). The most numerous, however, is pottery of the Kalenderberg culture, all of it dated to the Hallstatt period. In addition, several clay spindle whorls were found, a bronze ring, a three-sided bronze arrowhead also known from Molpír and attributed to nomadic peoples such as the Scythians, and also remarkable antler products such as plaques decorated with geometric ornament and various antler tools. All these finds fit the picture of occupation of the hillfort in the Early Iron Age.

children.text: The hillfort may have served as an important watch and trading point on the mountain pass, but Novák does not rule out the function of a local administrative centre in the period of the Hallstatt culture either. Unfortunately the hillfort has been, and still is, a target of looters, who recently even attacked an archaeologist at the hillfort. It will therefore be in all our interests if walkers and people interested in our history start coming to the hillfort more often, because the more people pass through it, the less peace the looters will have. An interesting find of an early La Tène belt clasp from the hillfort of Prašník – Tlstá hora.

From an article by K. Pieta of 2019:
 “The number of early La Tène find spots in the area of the Lesser Carpathians has been increased by an older chance find of an iron belt clasp, which it was possible to document together with other objects (Figs 1; 2). According to the data obtained, they come from the hillfort of Prašník, Tlstá hora (426 m), Trnava district, with intensive occupation of the Kalenderberg culture with Lusatian influences (Novák 2001; Veliačik/Romsauer 1994). The box-type iron clasp (a two-part clasp with a casing; Bujna 2011, 125, 127) is one of the typical components of the belt of female, but occasionally also male, costume of the early La Tène period (Fig. 3). They are especially common in a plain iron form without decoration (Frey 1996, 202, Figs 2; 6; Stöllner 2002, 96–98). The clasps of this type from the hillfort of Slepý vrch near Horné Orešany likewise belong predominantly to plain iron examples (Pieta 2007, 13, Fig. 10; Pieta/Jakubčinová/ Šebesta 2011, 212, Fig. 97: 10). The example from Prašník belongs to the variant with a large rectangular plate and a projecting hook, which formed part of the fastening of wider leather belts. It seems that the pieces with a projecting hook, including the find from Prašník, belong to the later variants, dated to the end of phase Lta or to the beginning of phase LtB1 (Bujna 2011, 125, 127), or possibly somewhat later still (Ramsl 2011, 105). The decoration of the clasp from Prašník was concentrated on its visible parts, on the upper part of the casing and on the riveted catch-plate. The hook has the shape of an animal head, a mask with narrow almond-shaped eyes and a plastic framing of the lines of the brows, emphasised by chiselled notching. The round nostrils evoke a powerful fantastic animal, a quadruped (bull, ram, boar).

The composition of the decorated surface corresponds very well to the early La Tène style, using antithetically (facing each other) placed figures that create a symmetrical composition of the scene. Pairs of griffins with a characteristic hooked beak, round or almond-shaped eyes and large pointed ears enter Celtic art as an orientalising motif as early as its earliest phase, when they are applied to openwork belt clasps and to other sumptuous products. For details of the decoration we find parallels on several artefacts of early Celtic art. The lines of meanders framing the central scene on the shorter sides of the casing are found, for example, on the bronze clasp from Schwabsburg (Frey 2002, 291) or on the clasp from Želkovice, Hořovice district (Megaw/Megaw 2001, Fig. 429B). A certain model for the example analysed here may be seen in the well-known bronze clasp from grave 17 at the Austrian cemetery of Herzogenburg-Ossarn, with a hook in the shape of an animal head and antithetically composed engraved figural decoration (Frey 2002, 288, Fig. 173). The figure of the griffin reached Celtic artistic craftsmanship from the Orient and, in a modified form (with the head of a bird of prey, an eagle, and the body of a quadruped, but without wings), it is one of the frequently used motifs throughout the territory of early Celtic civilisation, including its eastern part (Frey 2002, 201, 202; Szabó 2012, 693). In Celtic iconography the emphasis is evidently predominantly on the bird of prey, the eagle, which in mythological symbolism is identified with one of the chief deities of the Celtic pantheon, with Taranis. The motif of the head of a bird of prey with a pronounced downward-curving beak is among the frequent motifs, especially on brooches of the early La Tène period. They are also found at sites in western Slovakia and, exceptionally, in the mountain region as well (Fig. 4). An exclusive artefact of Celtic fine art from Horné Orešany has been added to the finds from Slovakia. It is the handle of a knife or razor with an applied figure of a griffin (Fig. 5)”
